guide.title: Castro Pretorio, Rome: The Baths of Diocletian, Porta Pia and the Quarter Built After 1870
guide.intro: Castro Pretorio is rione XVIII in Roma Capitale's list of Rome's 22 rioni, toponymic code 118. It is named for the Castra Praetoria, the camp of the Praetorian Guard, whose walls Aurelian built into his city wall and whose interior is an army barracks today. The Historic Centre of Rome was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1980. What a visitor comes for is Roman or nineteenth-century, often both at once: the Baths of Diocletian, with Michelangelo's basilica inside their frigidarium and three sites of the Museo Nazionale Romano in and beside them; Piazza della Repubblica, laid out on the curve of the baths' great exedra; Michelangelo's Porta Pia on Via XX Settembre; and a planned quarter of ministries, palazzi and theatres built after 1870. Termini station itself is in the neighbouring rione of Esquilino. This is the rione you come out of its Via Marsala side into.

sections.heading: The Baths of Diocletian and what was built into them
sections.body:
The Baths of Diocletian are the reason this quarter looks the way it does. Turismo Roma, Roma Capitale's tourism service, records that construction was begun by the emperor Maximian in 298 AD, that the complex was inaugurated between 305 and 306 and dedicated to Diocletian, that it covered 13 hectares and held up to 3,000 people, and that it remained in use until the middle of the 6th century, when the Gothic war interrupted its water supply. The address is Viale Enrico De Nicola 78.

Almost everything else on this side of the rione is something later built into the ruins. The frigidarium is now the Basilica di Santa Maria degli Angeli e dei Martiri: Turismo Roma says Pius IV decided on the church in 1561, prompted by the Sicilian priest Antonio Lo Duca, and gave it to Michelangelo, then 86 years old, who worked it into the Roman hall - over 90 metres long - without altering it and used the natatio for the apse. The floor carries the Linea Clementina, a bronze meridian line about 45 metres long, inaugurated in October 1702. A circular hall on the west side of the baths became the church of San Bernardo alle Terme, which Turismo Roma describes as windowless and lit only through the opening at the centre of its coffered dome. The octagonal hall in the western corner, at the junction with today's Via Parigi, holds the Museo dell'Arte Salvata, and the facade of a demolished church of 1754, Sant'Isidoro alle Terme, still stands beside it. The great exedra of the baths set the curve of Piazza della Repubblica, whose semicircular colonnade retraces its perimeter.

Three sites of the Museo Nazionale Romano are in this rione: the Roman antiquities section inside the baths, Palazzo Massimo alle Terme, and the Museo dell'Arte Salvata in the Octagonal Hall. Turismo Roma records that the museum was instituted in 1889. Every opening time given here is Roma Capitale republishing a state museum's information, attributed as such, and Turismo Roma itself tells visitors to check the museum's site.

sections.heading: Porta Pia, the walls and the quarter built after 1870
sections.body:
The northern edge of the rione is the Aurelian Wall, and two gates in it are the rione's. Turismo Roma records that Porta Pia replaced the older Porta Nomentana between 1561 and 1565 and is one of the eighteen gates of the Aurelian Walls, and that Pius IV gave the design to Michelangelo. Two Roma Capitale bodies disagree about who finished the gate, and both accounts are carried in its entry. On 20 September 1870 the Breccia was opened in the walls a few tens of metres from the gate; a marble monument of 1920 and a commemorative column mark the event, and Turismo Roma says the marks of the fighting are still visible on the walls and on the gate itself. Porta Pia has housed the Museo Storico dei Bersaglieri since 1932. Italian Wikipedia says that Porta Nomentana, on Viale del Policlinico, was walled up in 1564 when Porta Pia opened, and that it now forms part of the perimeter wall of the British Embassy compound.

The older Servian Wall crosses this quarter too, but the Sovrintendenza Capitolina says its most monumental remains are the ones beside Termini station, at the former Porta Viminalis, and those are in Esquilino. One stretch, near Via Gaeta and Via Volturno, is in this rione, and that is the one this guide claims.

Between the wall and the baths is a planned nineteenth-century quarter that reads as a single piece. The Palazzo delle Finanze at Via XX Settembre 97 and Palazzo Esercito are the two ministries. Piazza dell'Indipendenza carries the Palazzo dei Marescialli of 1930, the Villino Centurini of 1874 and the Villino Semiradski, alongside two modernist blocks of the 1950s, the Palazzo della Federconsorzi and the Palazzo del Corriere dello Sport. Italian Wikipedia's article on the rione records that Via Cernaia carries bronzes of Quintino Sella and Silvio Spaventa, by Emilio Gallori in 1893 and Giulio Tadolini in 1898, and dates the church of the Santissimo Rosario di Pompei on the same street to 1889-1898. The Teatro dell'Opera di Roma, opened in 1880 as the Teatro Costanzi, faces Piazza Beniamino Gigli; the Teatro Nazionale, built in 1925 as the Supercinema, is on Via del Viminale and is the opera company's second house. The Biblioteca Nazionale Centrale di Roma is at Viale Castro Pretorio 105: Italian Wikipedia attributes it to Massimo Castellazzi, Tullio Dell'Anese and Annibale Vitellozzi and dates its occupation to 1975.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
Termini is the arrival for almost everyone and it is not in this rione. The station building, its forecourt and Piazza dei Cinquecento are in Esquilino, and Italian Wikipedia's article on the square calls it al confine tra i rioni Esquilino e Castro Pretorio. The rione's own boundary description runs the line along Via Marsala and Piazza dei Cinquecento. Leave Termini by the Via Marsala side and you are in Castro Pretorio: the Basilica del Sacro Cuore di Gesu stands on that street, and the Castra Praetoria is behind it.

The other pole of the rione is Piazza della Repubblica, with Santa Maria degli Angeli e dei Martiri in the frigidarium of the baths and the Fontana delle Naiadi at its centre. The Baths of Diocletian are at Viale Enrico De Nicola 78; Turismo Roma publishes Palazzo Massimo's address as Largo di Villa Peretti 1 and the Museo dell'Arte Salvata's as Via Giuseppe Romita 8.

From Piazza della Repubblica, Via XX Settembre runs past the ministries to Porta Pia. Italian Wikipedia's article on the rione names Via XX Settembre as part of the boundary with Trevi and Sallustiano, so the buildings along it are not all in one rione - and neither are the four churches on and around Piazza San Bernardo. San Bernardo alle Terme and the Fontana del Mose are Castro Pretorio's; Santa Susanna, on the same square, is not this rione's; Santa Maria della Vittoria opposite is in Sallustiano. Where Via delle Quattro Fontane meets Via XX Settembre, the Palazzo Mattei Albani Del Drago is in this rione.

Opening hours are the weak point here. Where hours appear here they are either the institution's own - the Basilica di Santa Maria degli Angeli publishes its own, and announced a reopening after restoration for Sunday 6 September - or Roma Capitale republishing a state museum's, said to be such. San Bernardo alle Terme, St Paul's Within the Walls and the Russian church of San Nicola have telephone numbers published by Turismo Roma and no hours at all. Check before travelling.

faq.question: Is Termini station in Castro Pretorio?
faq.answer: No. Termini is in the neighbouring rione of Esquilino. Italian Wikipedia's article on Piazza dei Cinquecento calls the square al confine tra i rioni Esquilino e Castro Pretorio and tags it to both. What is in Castro Pretorio is the Via Marsala side: the Basilica del Sacro Cuore di Gesu stands on that street and the Castra Praetoria is behind it. Neither the station nor Piazza dei Cinquecento is covered in this guide.

faq.question: Four churches stand on and around Piazza San Bernardo. Which of them are in this rione?
faq.answer: Two things on that square are Castro Pretorio's: the church of San Bernardo alle Terme and the Fontana del Mose. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina's own record for the fountain carries a Rione field and it reads Castro Pretorio. Santa Susanna, on the same square, is not this rione's. Santa Maria della Vittoria opposite, with Bernini's Ecstasy of Saint Teresa, is in Sallustiano and is written up in the Sallustiano guide. The boundary runs through the square, which is why four churches a guidebook treats as one stop are not all in one guide.

faq.question: How many Museo Nazionale Romano sites are in this rione?
faq.answer: Three: the Roman antiquities section inside the Baths of Diocletian at Viale Enrico De Nicola 78, Palazzo Massimo alle Terme, published by Turismo Roma at Largo di Villa Peretti 1, and the Museo dell'Arte Salvata in the Octagonal Hall at Via Giuseppe Romita 8. Turismo Roma records that the museum was instituted in 1889. Every opening time here comes from Roma Capitale republishing the state museum's information, and Turismo Roma itself directs visitors to the museum's site for updates. Check before travelling.

faq.question: Can you go inside the Castra Praetoria?
faq.answer: No. The ground of the Praetorian camp is a working barracks of the Esercito Italiano on Viale Castro Pretorio and is not open to visitors. What you can see is the wall. Italian Wikipedia's article on the Castra Praetoria dates the camp to 21-23 AD under Tiberius and gives its extent as 440 by 380 metres, and Aurelian later absorbed its walls into his circuit, so the camp's northern and eastern sides stand today as part of the city wall.

faq.question: Who built Porta Pia?
faq.answer: Two Roma Capitale bodies answer that differently, and this guide reports both rather than picking one. Turismo Roma says Pius IV gave the design to Michelangelo, that it was among his last works of architecture, and that after his death in 1564 the project passed to Giacomo Del Duca. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina, describing the same gate, says Michelangelo completed only the inner front and that the gate was finished in the 19th century by Virginio Vespignani. Turismo Roma adds that the attic and the outer facade toward Via Nomentana are 19th-century and unconnected to Michelangelo's project.

faq.question: The British Embassy is on Via XX Settembre. Is it foreign territory?
faq.answer: No. The British Embassy is at Via XX Settembre 80/a, 00187 Rome, and GOV.UK states that public access to embassies, high commissions and consulates is by appointment only. It is not a visitor place and it has no entry in this guide. The compound stands on Italian soil: diplomatic premises are inviolable under the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, which is not the same thing as being foreign territory, and visitors and neighbours there are under Italian law. The same is true of the Russian embassy. Italian Wikipedia records that the walled-up Porta Nomentana now forms part of the perimeter wall of the British Embassy compound.

photos.title: Porta Pia
photos.description: The city-side front of Porta Pia, the gate in the Aurelian Walls built between 1561 and 1565 to Michelangelo's design, on Via XX Settembre.
photos.author: Dietmar Rabich

places.name: Terme di Diocleziano
places.address: Viale Enrico De Nicola 78, Roma RM
places.summary: The remains of the imperial baths that set the shape of this whole quarter, begun under Maximian in 298 AD.
places.history:
Turismo Roma, Roma Capitale's tourism service, records that construction of the Baths of Diocletian was begun by the emperor Maximian in 298 AD and that the complex was inaugurated between 305 and 306 and dedicated to Diocletian, with whom Maximian shared command of the empire. Turismo Roma gives the extent as 13 hectares and the capacity as up to 3,000 people, and says the central axis of calidarium, tepidarium and frigidarium is still legible in the Basilica of Santa Maria degli Angeli e dei Martiri. The complex remained in use until the middle of the 6th century, when the Gothic war interrupted its water supply.

Turismo Roma also places the octagonal hall of the baths in the western corner, at the junction with today's Via Parigi, and says that a circular hall on the west side of the complex was turned into the church of San Bernardo alle Terme. Almost everything a visitor sees on this side of the rione is something later built into, or against, these ruins.

places.name: Castra Praetoria
places.summary: The camp of the Praetorian Guard, which gives the rione its name and whose walls Aurelian built into the city wall.
places.history: The rione takes its name from the Castra Praetoria, the camp of the Praetorian Guard. Italian Wikipedia's article on the Castra Praetoria dates its construction to 21-23 AD under Tiberius and gives its extent as 440 by 380 metres. Aurelian later absorbed its walls into his circuit, which is why the camp's northern and eastern sides survive as part of the city wall. Those two sides are what a visitor can actually see; the interior of the camp is a working barracks and is covered separately in this guide.

places.name: Caserma Castro Pretorio (Caserma Macao)
places.summary: The working army barracks that occupies the ground of the Praetorian camp. It is not open to visitors.
places.history: The ancient camp is occupied today by a working barracks of the Esercito Italiano on Viale Castro Pretorio. It is not open to visitors. No source states more about the barracks, so nothing further is given here.

places.name: Porta Pia
places.summary: A gate in the Aurelian Walls, whose design Turismo Roma says Pius IV gave to Michelangelo, and the ground of the Breccia of 20 September 1870.
places.history:
Turismo Roma records that Porta Pia replaced the older Porta Nomentana between 1561 and 1565 and is one of the eighteen gates of the Aurelian Walls. Pope Pius IV gave the design to Michelangelo; it was among his last works of architecture, and after his death in 1564 the project passed to the architect Giacomo Del Duca. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina, describing the same gate, says instead that Michelangelo completed only the inner front and that the gate was finished in the 19th century by the architect Virginio Vespignani. Both are Roma Capitale bodies and the corpus reports both. Turismo Roma adds that the designs of the attic and of the outer facade toward Via Nomentana are 19th-century and unconnected to Michelangelo's project.

On 20 September 1870 the Breccia was opened in the walls a few tens of metres from the gate; a marble monument of 1920 and a commemorative column mark the event, and Turismo Roma says the marks of the fighting are still visible on the walls and on the gate itself. The Monumento al Bersagliere by the sculptor Publio Morbiducci was placed in the middle of the piazzale outside the gate in 1932. The gate itself has housed the Museo Storico dei Bersaglieri since 1932, which has its own entry here.

places.name: Porta Nomentana
places.summary: A gate of Aurelian's original circuit, walled up in 1564 when Porta Pia opened.
places.history: Porta Nomentana, on Viale del Policlinico, was part of Aurelian's original circuit and was walled up in 1564, when Porta Pia opened, according to Italian Wikipedia, which also says the walled-up gate now forms part of the perimeter wall of the British Embassy compound. The embassy stands on Italian soil; diplomatic premises are inviolable under the Vienna Convention but are not foreign territory.

places.name: Mura Serviane (Servian Wall)
places.summary: The republican city wall of yellow tufa. One stretch of it, near Via Gaeta and Via Volturno, falls inside this rione.
places.history: The Sovrintendenza Capitolina describes the Servian Wall as surviving in large blocks of yellow tufa. It dates the oldest circuit to the 6th century BC and attributes it to Servius Tullius, but says most of what survives belongs to the rebuilding of the early 4th century BC, shortly after the sack of Rome by the Gauls in 390 BC - a dating supported by the use of a particular tufa, tufo giallo di Grotta Oscura, quarried in territory controlled by the Etruscan city of Veii, whose heavy use in Rome must therefore postdate the conquest of Veii in 396 BC. The Sovrintendenza gives the circuit as about 11 km enclosing 426 hectares, and says that from the Porta Collina to the Porta Esquilina, where the ground is flat, an agger of ditch and rampart reinforced the wall. The Sovrintendenza states that the most monumental surviving remains are those beside Termini station, at the former Porta Viminalis - those are in the neighbouring rione of Esquilino, not here. One further stretch, near Via Gaeta and Via Volturno, falls inside Castro Pretorio.

places.name: Museo Nazionale Romano - Terme di Diocleziano
places.address: Viale Enrico De Nicola 78, Roma RM
places.summary: The Roman antiquities section of the Museo Nazionale Romano, inside part of the Baths of Diocletian.
places.history: Turismo Roma records that the Museo Nazionale Romano was instituted in 1889 and that part of the Baths has housed its Roman antiquities section since that year, with the finds arranged by topographic criterion and the garden holding funerary epigraphy and architecture. Turismo Roma republishes the opening hours as closed on Monday, with last entry at 18.00, and directs visitors to the museum's own site for updates.

places.name: Museo Nazionale Romano - Palazzo Massimo alle Terme
places.address: Largo di Villa Peretti 1, Roma RM
places.summary: The sculpture, coin and Roman painting galleries of the Museo Nazionale Romano, in a neo-Cinquecento palace of the 1880s.
places.history:
Turismo Roma gives the museum's address as Largo di Villa Peretti 1. Italian Wikipedia dates the building 1883-1886; Turismo Roma dates it 1883-1887 and names Camillo Pistrucci as its architect, working in a neo-Cinquecento style on ground previously occupied by the Villa Peretti built by Sixtus V and later a Massimo family residence. The State acquired it in 1981 and converted it to exhibition space.

Turismo Roma names among the holdings the former Museo Kircheriano material, the Gnecchi and Savoia collections, the Vittorio Emanuele III collection of medieval and modern coins and a goldwork section; and, among the sculpture, the Augustus as Pontifex Maximus from Via Labicana, the Fanciulla di Anzio, the Discobolus Lancellotti, the Sleeping Hermaphroditus, the Doidalsas Venus about to bathe and the Apollo del Tevere. On the second floor are the frescoes from the Villa of Livia at Prima Porta, and four rooms of the nine surviving from the Villa della Farnesina, dated to about 20 BC, are reconstructed there.

Turismo Roma republishes the opening hours as Tuesday to Sunday 9.30 to 19.00, with the ticket office closing at 18.00 and the museum closed on Monday. The published address is on a largo whose northern end lies in the neighbouring rione of Esquilino; the museum building itself is in Castro Pretorio.

places.name: Museo Nazionale Romano - Museo dell'Arte Salvata (Aula Ottagona)
places.summary: The Museo Nazionale Romano's display of recovered antiquities, in the Octagonal Hall of the Baths of Diocletian.
places.history: Turismo Roma records that the Museo dell'Arte Salvata occupies the Aula Ottagona of the Museo Nazionale Romano - Terme di Diocleziano, at Via Giuseppe Romita 8. Turismo Roma's separate page for the Baths of Diocletian places that octagonal hall in the western corner of the complex, at the junction with today's Via Parigi, which is the one independent Roma Capitale confirmation of where it stands. Turismo Roma republishes the ticket office closing time as 18.00 and the museum as closed on Monday.

places.name: Museo Storico dei Bersaglieri
places.summary: The regimental museum of the Bersaglieri, housed inside Porta Pia since 1932.
places.history: The Sovrintendenza Capitolina states that Porta Pia has housed the Museo Storico dei Bersaglieri since 1932, and that the museum holds relics of the Corps' foundation, of the Risorgimento campaigns and of both world wars, with a Sacrario dedicated to more than 100,000 fallen on the ground floor. Turismo Roma gives the museum's inauguration date as 18 September 1932 and describes the floors in turn: the Risorgimento campaigns of 1848 to 1866 on the first floor, the colonial campaigns above, the First World War below and the Second World War on the ground floor, with bronze busts of the Corps' figures in the courtyard. The museum is run by the Esercito Italiano. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.

places.name: Biblioteca Nazionale Centrale di Roma Vittorio Emanuele II
places.summary: One of Italy's two national central libraries, in a Movimento Moderno building occupied from 1975.
places.history: The Biblioteca Nazionale Centrale di Roma Vittorio Emanuele II is at Viale Castro Pretorio 105, 00185 Rome. Italian Wikipedia describes it as one of Italy's two national central libraries alongside the Biblioteca Nazionale Centrale di Firenze, records that it was instituted in the 1870s and originally housed in the Collegio Romano, and attributes the present building, occupied from 1975, to Massimo Castellazzi, Tullio Dell'Anese and Annibale Vitellozzi, working in the idiom of the Movimento Moderno. Italian Wikipedia also says three exhibition areas in the atrium are open to the public, among them the Museo Spazi900, whose permanent centrepiece, La stanza di Elsa, recreates Elsa Morante's writing room from her original furniture. No source states the library's hours, holdings figures or access conditions, so none are given here.

places.name: MuSEd - Museo della Scuola e dell'Educazione Mauro Laeng
places.summary: A university museum of the history of pedagogy, run by the Universita Roma Tre.
places.history: The MuSEd, the Museo della Scuola e dell'Educazione Mauro Laeng, is run by the Dipartimento di Scienze della Formazione of the Universita Roma Tre, whose own site confirms the department. Italian Wikipedia describes it as a museum of the history of pedagogy, founded in 1874 and opened in its present form in 1986, and gives its address as Piazza della Repubblica 10; the department is also recorded at Via del Castro Pretorio 20. No source settles which of the two is current, so both are given as reported rather than one being chosen.

places.name: Basilica di Santa Maria degli Angeli e dei Martiri
places.summary: Michelangelo's church inside the frigidarium of the Baths of Diocletian, with a bronze meridian line about 45 metres long set in its floor.
places.history:
Turismo Roma records that in 1561 Pius IV, prompted by the Sicilian priest Antonio Lo Duca, decided to build a church inside the Baths of Diocletian, and that the commission went to Michelangelo, then 86 years old. Michelangelo worked the church into the Roman rectangular hall, over 90 metres long, without altering it, used the natatio for the apse, and made the concave brick facade out of an exedra of the calidarium. After his death on 18 February 1564 the work continued under Jacopo Del Duca, his pupil and Lo Duca's nephew.

The floor carries the Meridiana, or Linea Clementina, inaugurated in October 1702 under Clement XI and made by Francesco Bianchini: a bronze line about 45 metres long set in a band of marble. Luigi Vanvitelli reworked the church in 1750 and built the facade toward Piazza Esedra, which was demolished in 1911 to bring the niche of the calidarium back into view. In 1998 the Comune di Roma gave the basilica a new monumental organ by Bartolomeo Formentelli of Verona, and in 2001 Narcissus Quagliata installed a stained-glass dome 5 metres across at a height of 23 metres, which also works as a meridian.

The basilica publishes its own hours: Monday to Friday 8:00-13:00 and 16:00-19:00, Saturday, Sunday and holidays 10:00-13:00 and 16:00-19:00. Mass is at 18:30 Monday to Saturday; on Sunday at 9:00 in English, 10:30, 12:00 and 18:30 in Italian, and 17:00 in Spanish. Confessions are heard daily from 10:00 to 12:00 and after each Mass. The basilica has been closed for restoration and announced its reopening on these hours for Sunday 6 September; check the parish's site before travelling.

places.name: Basilica del Sacro Cuore di Gesu a Castro Pretorio
places.summary: The Salesian minor basilica in Via Marsala, completed in 1887 through St John Bosco, with his last Roman rooms behind the choir.
places.history:
The basilica stands in Via Marsala. Italian Wikipedia records that Pius IX laid the first stone in 1870, that work stopped at the annexation of Rome and resumed in 1880 through St John Bosco, and that the church was completed in 1887 to a design by the architect Francesco Vespignani. The parish was erected on 2 February 1879 by the vicarial decree Postremis hisce temporibus; Benedict XV raised the church to the rank of minor basilica on 11 February 1921 by the apostolic letter Pia societas; and Paul VI created the cardinal deaconry on 5 February 1965.

Behind the choir the Salesians preserve the rooms known as le Camerette di Don Bosco. Italian Wikipedia records that Don Bosco stayed there from 30 April to 18 May 1887, on the twentieth and last of his journeys to Rome, for the consecration of the basilica; that the space was originally two rooms, a study where he received visitors and a bedroom with a cabinet altar for private Mass; and that the wall between them was later demolished to make a single chapel as pilgrims began to come.

No source states a street number, opening hours or Mass times for the basilica, so none are given here.

places.name: Chiesa di San Bernardo alle Terme
places.summary: A circular hall of the Baths of Diocletian turned into a church in 1598, windowless and lit only through the oculus of its dome.
places.history:
Turismo Roma says the church stands on the perimeter of one of the circular towers that rose beside the remains of the Baths of Diocletian, and that in 1598 the countess Caterina Sforza Cesarini had it turned into a church. It is cylindrical and entirely without windows, lit only through the circular opening at the centre of an octagonally coffered dome, and measures 22 metres across inside. Eight raised niches hold stucco saints by Camillo Mariani, made around 1600 and each more than three metres tall: Augustine, Monica, Mary Magdalene, Francis, Bernard, Catherine of Alexandria, Catherine of Siena and Jerome. The two altarpieces are by Giovanni Odazzi. The church was first entrusted to the French Cistercians known as the Feuillants; after the French Revolution the order was dissolved and San Bernardo passed to the congregation of Bernard of Clairvaux, to whom it is dedicated. The Cappella di San Francesco holds the funerary monument of the German painter Friedrich Overbeck, founder of the Nazarenes, and the organ in the apse is by Nicola Morettini, 1885. Turismo Roma publishes a telephone number, 06 4882122, and no opening hours, directing visitors to the contacts given.

One thing a guidebook will get wrong here. Santa Susanna, on the same square, is not this rione's; Santa Maria della Vittoria opposite is in Sallustiano.

places.name: Chiesa di San Paolo dentro le Mura (St Paul's Within the Walls)
places.summary: The American Episcopal church built between 1873 and 1880 by the English architect George Edmond Street.
places.history: St Paul's Within the Walls, in Italian the Chiesa di San Paolo dentro le Mura, stands at Via Nazionale 16a, with a side entrance on Via Napoli. Italian Wikipedia says it was built between 1873 and 1880 by the English architect George Edmond Street for Rome's American Episcopal community, at the initiative of the Reverend Robert J. Nevin, in a neo-Romanesque and neo-Gothic manner using red Sienese brick alternating with travertine. Turismo Roma publishes a telephone number, 06 4883339, and no opening hours.

places.name: Chiesa del Santissimo Rosario di Pompei
places.summary: A neoclassical church of 1889-1898 in Via Cernaia, with the Marist Fathers' provincial curia attached.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia's article on the rione gives the church's name as Chiesa del Santissimo Rosario di Pompei; OpenStreetMap carries the double dedication Santa Maria del Rosario e San Pietro Chanel as an alternative. Italian Wikipedia says it was built between 1889 and 1898 to a neoclassical design by Pio Piacentini, with the provincial curia of the Marist Fathers and an international student hostel attached. Both statements are an aggregator's and are attributed as such; no first-party source states it.

places.name: Chiesa russa di San Nicola Taumaturgo
places.summary: The Russian Orthodox parish church of Rome, in Via Palestro.
places.history: Turismo Roma publishes the address of the Russian church of San Nicola Taumaturgo as Via Palestro 69/71, together with a telephone number, 06 4450729, and no opening hours. The parish's own site, which is in Russian, describes it as the Russian Orthodox parish church in Rome. Italian Wikipedia has no article on it, so its link from the article on the rione is a red link.

places.name: Chiesa evangelica metodista in Castro Pretorio
places.summary: The Methodist church of Rome, at the corner of Via XX Settembre and Via Firenze, consecrated in 1895.
places.history: Turismo Roma gives the address as Via XX Settembre 123; the church stands at the corner of Via Firenze. Italian Wikipedia says it was built between 1893 and 1895 and consecrated on 20 September 1895, on ground cleared by the master plan of 1881 and on the site of the demolished church of San Caio. The rione article's own list of vanished churches independently names San Caio, Santa Teresa alle Quattro Fontane and the Santissima Incarnazione del Verbo Divino, which is the same clearance seen from the other side. No coordinate is given: Turismo Roma gives the identical point for this church and for Palazzo Esercito, so at most one of the two can be right.

places.name: Facciata di Sant'Isidoro alle Terme
places.summary: The surviving facade of a church of 1754, demolished in 1940 to bring the Baths of Diocletian back into view.
places.history: Beside the Octagonal Hall, on Via Parigi, stands the surviving facade of the church of Sant'Isidoro alle Terme. Italian Wikipedia records that Benedict XIV had the church built in 1754 to a design by Giuseppe Pannini, using rooms next to the Octagonal Hall that had served the popes as grain stores, and that the church was deconsecrated and then demolished in 1940 so that the remains of the Baths could be brought back to view. The facade on Via Parigi remains; one small interior room survives and, as of 2023, is not open to the public.

places.name: Piazza della Repubblica
places.summary: The square laid out on the line of the great exedra of the Baths of Diocletian, framed by Gaetano Koch's colonnades.
places.history: Turismo Roma records that the square took its old name, Piazza Esedra, from the great exedra of the Baths of Diocletian, whose perimeter its semicircular colonnade retraces, and that the colonnade and the palaces that frame it are the work of the Turin architect Gaetano Koch, in the late 19th century. Italian Wikipedia's article on the rione describes them as the two great porticoed Savoyard palaces at the sides, following the line of the baths' exedra. The Basilica di Santa Maria degli Angeli e dei Martiri opens off the square and the Fontana delle Naiadi stands at its centre; both have their own entries here.

places.name: Fontana delle Naiadi
places.summary: The fountain at the centre of Piazza della Repubblica, the terminal display of the Acqua Pia Antica Marcia, with Mario Rutelli's bronze nymphs.
places.history:
The Sovrintendenza Capitolina's record for this fountain carries a Rione field and it reads Castro Pretorio - the plainest statement of the rione anywhere in this guide. The Sovrintendenza describes the fountain as the mostra, or terminal display, of the Acqua Pia Antica Marcia, the aqueduct built between 1865 and 1870 under Pius IX. It names Alessandro Guerrieri and Mario Rutelli as the authors, dates the work 1885-1914, and lists granite, travertine, bronze and cement conglomerate as the materials.

The Sovrintendenza records that the pope provisionally inaugurated the aqueduct's display on 10 September 1870, in the Termini area, and that the fountain was then built definitively in what is now Piazza della Repubblica: the architecture by Guerrieri in 1885, temporarily dressed with four stucco lions for the visit of Wilhelm II in 1888. Rutelli was commissioned for the sculpture in 1897 and the fountain was inaugurated in 1901. A first central group in cement, of 1911, was rejected and moved in 1913 to the garden of Piazza Vittorio Emanuele II; the Glauco clasping a dolphin replaced it and was inaugurated in 1914. The Sovrintendenza records a full restoration in 1998 and another in 2025 under the PNRR - Caput Mundi programme.

Turismo Roma names the four nymphs and their creatures: the Nymph of the Oceans with a sea-horse, of the Rivers with a water-snake, of the Lakes with a swan and of the Subterranean Waters with a lizard. Turismo Roma alone describes the rejected central group as three tritons, a dolphin and an octopus.

places.name: Fontana del Mose
places.summary: The terminal display of the Acquedotto Felice on Piazza San Bernardo, built for Sixtus V between 1585 and 1589.
places.history:
The Sovrintendenza Capitolina's record for this fountain also carries a Rione field reading Castro Pretorio. The Sovrintendenza says the fountain was erected between 1585 and 1589 as the terminal mostra of the Acquedotto Felice, willed by Sixtus V - Felice Peretti, from whom the aqueduct takes its name - and gives the authors as Giovanni Fontana and Domenico Fontana, in travertine, marble and stucco, in the form of a triumphal arch of three bays. The colossal Moses is by Prospero Antichi, finished by Leonardo Sormani; the side reliefs are of Aaron by Gian Battista della Porta and of Gideon by Pietro Paolo Olivieri and Flaminio Vacca. The four antique porphyry and marble lions at the basins were replaced in 1850 by bardiglio lions by Adamo Tadolini. The travertine balustrade was made under Pius IV for the Belvedere courtyard in the Vatican and reused here. The cornice carries the dates 1585-1587. The Sovrintendenza records restorations in 1850-51 and 1987-89 and maintenance in 2010-11.

One caution: Turismo Roma has a separate record called Acquedotto Felice, but it points at Via Lemonia in the Parco degli Acquedotti, on the other side of the city. It is not this fountain and the two should not be joined.

places.name: Monumento ai Caduti di Dogali
places.summary: An Egyptian obelisk of Ramses II, reused in 1887 as the memorial to the 548 soldiers killed at Dogali.
places.history:
The Sovrintendenza Capitolina records that the monument commemorates the 548 soldiers who died at Dogali, in Eritrea, on 26 January 1887, under Lieutenant Colonel Tommaso De Cristoforis, against the Ethiopian imperial forces of ras Alula. It was designed by Francesco Azzurri (1827-1901). The city council resolved on it in February 1887 on the proposal of Ruggiero Bonghi, made in the newspaper L'Opinione, and at the suggestion of the mayor, Leopoldo Torlonia, reused the Egyptian obelisk of Ramses II found in 1883 in Rodolfo Lanciani's excavation of the Iseo Campense. On 9 March 1887 the Giunta sited it in the square in front of Termini station, which the Sovrintendenza says has been named for the Cinquecento ever since. That square is in the neighbouring rione of Esquilino and is not claimed here; the monument stands in the garden between Via delle Terme di Diocleziano and Via Luigi Einaudi, where it was moved between July 1924 and 31 May 1925 for tram works before the Jubilee of 1925, with a new setting by the municipal architect Raffaele de Vico (1881-1969). It was inaugurated on 5 June 1887. The Sovrintendenza gives the obelisk as Aswan granite; Turismo Roma calls it red granite and over 9 metres tall, and adds that its twin is in the Boboli gardens and that its tip was found by chance in 1719 during foundation work at the Biblioteca Casanatense.

The Sovrintendenza Capitolina records that after the Italian conquest of Ethiopia in 1935-36 the Lion of Judah - a gilded bronze sculpture given to the Negus in 1929 by the Societe Technique et Industrielle d'Entreprises for the opening of the passenger service at the Ethiopian capital's railway station - was brought to Rome as war booty. In March 1937 the proposal of Antonio Munoz, director of the Governatorato's antiquities and fine arts division, to place the lion on the base of the Dogali monument was accepted, and the new arrangement was inaugurated on 9 May that year. The city administration decided to remove the sculpture in 1943; it was held at the Antiquarium del Celio until 1970, when it was officially returned to the Ethiopian government.

The Sovrintendenza also records a restoration of the monument and its historic garden between 2024 and 2025, carried out by the Soprintendenza Speciale Archeologia Belle Arti e Paesaggio di Roma under the PNRR.

places.name: Monumento della Caravella (Colonna di Parigi)
places.summary: A cipollino marble column carrying a bronze caravel, given by Paris and erected in 1959.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia's article on the rione describes a column of cipollino marble topped by a bronze caravel, given by the city of Paris and erected in 1959 to commemorate the twinning of Rome and Paris of 9 April 1956, carrying the motto Solo Parigi e degna di Roma e solo Roma e degna di Parigi. The same article places the column on Via Parigi. Turismo Roma carries its own page for it under the name Colonna di Parigi, but gives a different street, Via Giuseppe Romita, so the street here is taken from one named source only and no address is published.

places.name: Monumento a Quintino Sella
places.summary: A bronze of the finance minister Quintino Sella in Via Cernaia, by Emilio Gallori, 1893.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia's article on the rione records the monument as a bronze by Emilio Gallori of 1893, in Via Cernaia. No dedicated article and no first-party source states it, so the entry rests on that single aggregator and is attributed accordingly.

places.name: Monumento a Silvio Spaventa
places.summary: A bronze of the statesman Silvio Spaventa in Via Cernaia, by Giulio Tadolini, 1898.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia's article on the rione records the monument as a bronze by Giulio Tadolini of 1898, in Via Cernaia. As with the Sella bronze on the same street, no dedicated article and no first-party source states it, and the entry is attributed to that one aggregator.

places.name: Piazza dell'Indipendenza
places.summary: The square of the quarter laid out after 1870, named for the Italian wars of independence like the streets around it.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia records that Piazza dell'Indipendenza belongs to the quarter built after 1870 and was named for the Italian wars of independence, as were the streets around it, and that Via Solferino crosses it with Via Goito and Via dei Mille. Turismo Roma also carries a page for the square. Five buildings on it are written up separately in this guide: the Palazzo dei Marescialli, the Villino Centurini, the Villino Semiradski, the Palazzo della Federconsorzi and the Palazzo del Corriere dello Sport.

places.name: Piazza Beniamino Gigli
places.summary: The square the Teatro dell'Opera di Roma faces.
places.history: This is the square in front of the opera house. Italian Wikipedia's article on the rione places the Teatro dell'Opera di Roma on it, and the theatre's own site names the square without publishing a street number, which is why no number appears in the theatre's entry either.

places.name: Teatro dell'Opera di Roma (Teatro Costanzi)
places.summary: Rome's opera house, opened in 1880 as the Teatro Costanzi, where Cavalleria rusticana and Tosca had their first performances.
places.history:
The Teatro dell'Opera di Roma publishes its own history of the building. It was built in 1879 for Domenico Costanzi (1810-1898), who gave the work to the Milanese architect Achille Sfondrini (1836-1900), and it went up in eighteen months on ground anciently occupied by the villa of Elagabalus. It was inaugurated on 27 November 1880 with Rossini's Semiramide, conducted by Giovanni Rossi before the sovereigns. Sfondrini designed the house as a cassa armonica, a sounding box, which is why the auditorium is a horseshoe; it held 2,212 seats in three tiers of boxes, an amphitheatre and a gallery, under a dome frescoed by Annibale Brugnoli.

Four operas had their world premieres here. The theatre's own account puts Cavalleria rusticana, on 17 May 1890, and L'amico Fritz, on 31 October 1891, under Domenico Costanzi's management, and Tosca, on 14 January 1900, and Le Maschere, on 17 January 1901, under the direction of his son Enrico. Management passed to Walter Mocchi in 1907 and to Emma Carelli in 1912. The Comune di Roma bought the theatre in 1926, renamed it the Teatro Reale dell'Opera and had it remodelled by Marcello Piacentini; it closed on 15 November 1926 and reopened on 27 February 1928 with Boito's Nerone, conducted by Gino Marinuzzi. It was rebuilt again in 1958.

Italian Wikipedia's article on the rione dates the building 1874-80 and credits Sfondrini and Piacentini jointly. The theatre's own account contradicts that and puts Piacentini's work in 1926-28; this guide follows the theatre on its own dates. Neither the theatre's history page nor its contacts page publishes a street address, so the square is given here and no number.

places.name: Teatro Nazionale
places.summary: The Teatro dell'Opera's second house, built in 1925 as a cinema called the Supercinema.
places.history: The Teatro Nazionale stands on Via del Viminale at the corner of Via Agostino Depretis. The Teatro dell'Opera di Roma, which runs it, records that it was born as a cinema called the Supercinema, built in 1925 within a pre-existing building; that its owner, commendatore Urbano Rattazzi, commissioned the design from the architects Arnaldo Foschini and Attilio Spaccarelli with the engineer Giacomo Giobbe; that the hall measured 36 metres by 30 and originally seated 2,500 between stalls and galleries; and that the interior was decorated in Italian liberty style with gilded stucco, paintings, stone and fabric. An orchestra pit indicates that variety and other live forms alternated with film. From the postwar years it was a cinema only. At the end of the 1990s the Comune di Roma acquired the Supercinema and handed it to the Fondazione Teatro dell'Opera di Roma as a second house.

places.name: Palazzo delle Finanze
places.summary: The finance ministry's palace on Via XX Settembre, holding two historic libraries.
places.history:
The Ministero dell'Economia e delle Finanze gives the address of the Palazzo delle Finanze as Via XX Settembre 97, 00187 Rome. Italian Wikipedia's article on the rione dates the building 1871-1876. The sources disagree on the architect: the rione article credits the engineer Raffaele Canevari, while Italian Wikipedia's separate article on the building names Francesco Pieroni, Ercole Rosa and Pietro Costa. Two articles of the same encyclopedia disagreeing with each other are not a source, and no third source names an architect.

The ministry's own pages record that the Biblioteca Storica is in the building, holding funds inherited from the Kingdom of Sardinia and other pre-unification states, and that the Biblioteca Luca Pacioli holds over 12,000 volumes together with runs of the Rendiconto generale dello Stato and of the Bilancio di Previsione from 1870 onward.

places.name: Palazzo Esercito
places.summary: The 19th-century palace on Via XX Settembre built for the Kingdom's Ministry of War, and since 2017 also the seat of the Defence General Staff.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia's article on the rione describes Palazzo Esercito as a 19th-century building, dated 1876-85, from a project by Bernardini and Garavaglia, built for the Kingdom of Italy's Ministry of War and the Army General Staff, and records that it has been the seat of the Stato Maggiore della Difesa since 22 February 2017. Italian Wikipedia's separate article on the building gives different dates, so only the century, the architects' surnames and the 2017 fact are carried here. No coordinate is published: Turismo Roma gives the same point for this palace and for the Methodist church on the same street, so at most one of the two is right. Palazzo Caprara and Palazzo Baracchini are in the rione of Trevi and are not covered in this guide.

places.name: Palazzo dei Marescialli
places.summary: The seat of the Consiglio Superiore della Magistratura, built in 1930 on Piazza dell'Indipendenza.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia's article on the rione dates the Palazzo dei Marescialli to 1930, credits Gennaro de Matteis, and records it as the seat of the Consiglio Superiore della Magistratura, on Piazza dell'Indipendenza.

places.name: Villino Centurini
places.summary: An 1874 villa on Piazza dell'Indipendenza, now a state secondary school.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia's article on the rione records the Villino Centurini as built in 1874 by the Swiss architect Kleffler for Alessandro Centurini, on Piazza dell'Indipendenza at Via Vittorio Bachelet, and says it now houses the liceo statale Niccolo Machiavelli. The architect's forename is left out here because Italian Wikipedia's two articles give it differently, Henry in one and Enrico in the other.

places.name: Villino Semiradski
places.summary: An eclectic 19th-century villa on Piazza dell'Indipendenza by Francesco Azzurri.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia's article on the rione describes the Villino Semiradski as eclectic and 19th-century, by Francesco Azzurri, and records that it now houses the Comando Carabinieri Banca d'Italia. Azzurri is the same architect who designed the Monumento ai Caduti di Dogali, also in this rione.

places.name: Palazzo della Federconsorzi
places.summary: A modernist office block of 1955-57 on Piazza dell'Indipendenza.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia's article on the rione describes the Palazzo della Federconsorzi as modernist, dates it 1955-57 and credits Ignazio Guidi and Giulio Sterbini. That one aggregator is the whole of the evidence carried here.

places.name: Palazzo del Corriere dello Sport
places.summary: A modernist block of 1956 on Piazza dell'Indipendenza by Attilio Lapadula.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia's article on the rione describes the Palazzo del Corriere dello Sport as modernist, dates it 1956 and credits Attilio Lapadula. As with its neighbour the Palazzo della Federconsorzi, that single aggregator is the whole of the evidence and is attributed as such.

places.name: Palazzo Nathan
places.summary: An eclectic apartment palace of 1889 on Via Torino by Cesare Janz.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia's article on the rione records Palazzo Nathan, on Via Torino, as eclectic, 19th-century, dated 1889 and built by Cesare Janz. Nothing further is given: the account connecting the building to Ernesto Nathan, and the description of its storeys, its caryatid window frames and its corner loggia, was found only on a blog, and a claim about who lived and died in a building needs better than that.

places.name: Palazzo Mattei Albani Del Drago
places.address: Via delle Quattro Fontane, Roma RM
places.summary: A Mannerist palace of 1587 by Domenico Fontana, carrying the Arno figure of the Quattro Fontane on its corner.
places.history:
Italian Wikipedia's article on the rione records the palace as Mannerist, dated 1587, built by Domenico Fontana for Muzio Mattei, on Via delle Quattro Fontane at Via XX Settembre. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina's page for the Quattro Fontane independently records that Muzio Mattei paid for the fountain on the corner of his own palace, later the property of the Albani Del Drago, and that this corner carries the figure of the Arno with a lion.

The Sovrintendenza records that the fountain on this corner was made under Sixtus V, attributes it to Domenico Fontana with Pietro Berrettini da Cortona, and dates the work to 1588-1593 and 1667-69. It was originally fed by the Acquedotto Felice, and the Sovrintendenza records that Muzio Mattei, like the other adjoining landowners, paid for it in exchange for a free concession of water.

entries.name: Terme di Diocleziano
entries.note: Begun under Maximian in 298 AD and inaugurated between 305 and 306, covering 13 hectares and holding up to 3,000 people, in use until the Gothic war interrupted the water supply in the mid-6th century.

entries.name: Basilica di Santa Maria degli Angeli e dei Martiri
entries.note: Michelangelo, then 86, worked the church into the frigidarium's Roman hall of over 90 metres without altering it and used the natatio for the apse; the bronze Linea Clementina in the floor was inaugurated in October 1702.

entries.name: Museo Nazionale Romano - Terme di Diocleziano
entries.note: The Roman antiquities section has occupied part of the baths since 1889, arranged by topographic criterion, with funerary epigraphy and architecture in the garden.

entries.name: Museo Nazionale Romano - Palazzo Massimo alle Terme
entries.note: Camillo Pistrucci's neo-Cinquecento palace of the 1880s holds the Discobolus Lancellotti, the Fanciulla di Anzio and, on the second floor, the frescoes from the Villa of Livia at Prima Porta.

entries.name: Museo Nazionale Romano - Museo dell'Arte Salvata (Aula Ottagona)
entries.note: Recovered antiquities shown in the octagonal hall in the western corner of the baths, at the junction with Via Parigi; the entrance is at Via Giuseppe Romita 8.

entries.name: Piazza della Repubblica
entries.note: Gaetano Koch's semicircular colonnade and its two porticoed palaces retrace the perimeter of the baths' great exedra, which gave the square its old name, Piazza Esedra.

entries.name: Fontana delle Naiadi
entries.note: The terminal display of the Acqua Pia Antica Marcia: Guerrieri's architecture of 1885, Mario Rutelli's four bronze nymphs inaugurated in 1901 and the Glauco clasping a dolphin added in 1914.

entries.name: Chiesa di San Bernardo alle Terme
entries.note: A circular tower of the baths turned into a church in 1598 by Caterina Sforza Cesarini, 22 metres across inside, windowless and lit through the opening at the centre of its coffered dome, with eight stucco saints by Camillo Mariani.

entries.name: Fontana del Mose
entries.note: Erected between 1585 and 1589 for Sixtus V as the terminal display of the Acquedotto Felice, a travertine arch of three bays carrying Prospero Antichi's colossal Moses and reliefs of Aaron and Gideon.

entries.name: Porta Pia
entries.note: Built between 1561 and 1565 to replace Porta Nomentana, one of the eighteen gates of the Aurelian Walls, with the design given by Pius IV to Michelangelo; marks of the fighting of 20 September 1870 are still visible on the walls and the gate.

entries.name: Castra Praetoria
entries.note: The Praetorian camp of 21-23 AD under Tiberius measured 440 by 380 metres; Aurelian absorbed its walls, so its northern and eastern sides stand today as city wall while the interior is a working barracks.

entries.name: Mura Serviane (Servian Wall)
entries.note: Large blocks of yellow tufa from the rebuilding of the early 4th century BC survive in one stretch near Via Gaeta and Via Volturno.

entries.name: Teatro dell'Opera di Roma (Teatro Costanzi)
entries.note: Achille Sfondrini built it in eighteen months for Domenico Costanzi as a sounding box with a horseshoe auditorium, inaugurated on 27 November 1880 with Rossini's Semiramide; Cavalleria rusticana and Tosca had their world premieres here.

entries.name: Basilica del Sacro Cuore di Gesu a Castro Pretorio
entries.note: First stone laid by Pius IX in 1870, work resumed in 1880 through St John Bosco and completed in 1887; behind the choir are the rooms where he stayed from 30 April to 18 May 1887.

links.note: Sallustiano adjoins Castro Pretorio along Via XX Settembre. Santa Maria della Vittoria, at Via XX Settembre 17, is Sallustiano's and not this rione's.
Ludovisi is rione XVI in Roma Capitale's list of Rome's 22 rioni; Castro Pretorio is rione XVIII.
Prati is rione XXII in Roma Capitale's list of Rome's 22 rioni; Castro Pretorio is rione XVIII.
A three-day Rome itinerary based on Piazza della Repubblica, which is in this rione.
